### https://fortune.com/2023/06/09/mark-zuckerberg-elon-musk-twitter-meta-layoffs-middle-managers/
# Zuckerberg credits Musk with kicking off tech trend of firing middle managers | Fortune

Mark Zuckerberg is giving credit where credit is due. The Meta CEO believes that Elon Musk, by firing hordes of middle managers at Twitter after his $44 billion takeover last October, kicked off a trend that’s been “good for the industry.” 

After assuming control, Musk laid off thousands of employees, reducing headcount from about 7,500 to less than 2,000 by February of this year, [according to](https://techcrunch.com/2023/05/25/elon-musk-twitter-everything-you-need-to-know/) TechCrunch.

Zuckerberg delivered the comments [on the _Lex Fridman Podcast_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ff4fRgnuFgQ) on Thursday. The way he sees it—and laid-off Twitter employees would surely beg to differ—Musk was right in trying to make the company “more technical” and decrease the distance between engineers and himself, with “fewer layers of management.” 

“His actions led me and I think a lot of other folks in the industry to think about, ‘Hey, are we kind of doing this as much as we should?’” he said. “Could we make our companies better by pushing on some of the same principles?…My sense is that there were a lot of other people who thought that those were good changes, but who may have been a little shy about doing them.” 

It was something Musk “was quite ahead of a bunch of the other companies on,” he added.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, [announced in March](https://fortune.com/2023/03/14/meta-layoffs-10000-mark-zuckerberg-year-of-efficiency-hiring-freeze/) that it would lay off 10,000 employees—adding to the 11,000 job cuts it started last November—and would also freeze hiring on 5,000 more positions. In a [blog post](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/03/mark-zuckerberg-meta-year-of-efficiency/), Zuckerberg said he would “make our organization flatter by removing multiple layers of management,” part of a “year of efficiency.”

While Meta employees have [described “shattered” morale](https://fortune.com/2023/04/20/meta-employees-tech-layoffs-mark-zuckerberg-morale-confidence/), Wall Street has responded positively, with Meta shares up about 112% year to date.

Other big tech companies have [also shed workers this year](https://fortune.com/2023/01/07/salesforce-ceo-marc-benioff-dodges-layoffs-questions-ohana-mantra-questioned/), among them [Salesforce](https://fortune.com/company/salesforce-com/), [Microsoft](https://fortune.com/company/microsoft/), and [Amazon](https://fortune.com/company/amazon-com/). Tech layoffs in 2023 are [the highest they’ve been](https://fortune.com/2023/06/01/tech-layoffs-worst-since-dot-com-bubble-burst/) since the dotcom bubble burst 22 years ago, according to a [report](https://www.challengergray.com/blog/may-2023-layoffs-jump-on-tech-retail-auto-ytd-hiring-lowest-since-2016/) released earlier this month by recruiting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

Part of the problem was that many tech companies had simply over-hired in recent years, both because the pandemic increased demand for their products and services and because it was a period of easy money given Fed-induced low interest rates.

Stewart Butterfield, former CEO of Slack, recently [described a dynamic](https://fortune.com/2023/05/28/ex-slack-ceo-stewart-butterfield-tech-over-hiring-root-of-excess/) within tech companies behind much of the over-hiring. He noted on Bloomberg’s _Odd Lots_ [podcast](https://omny.fm/shows/odd-lots/slack-founder-stewart-butterfield-on-ai-software-a) in late May that when there’s no real constraint on hiring, “you hire someone, and the first thing that person wants to do is hire other people.” The reason is that “the more people who report to you, the higher your prestige, the more your power in the organization…So every budgeting process is, ‘I really want to hire,’ and that to me is the root of all the excess.”

Zuckerberg said it was “very hard to know” from the outside whether Musk fired too many or not enough workers at Twitter, but said the trend he helped kick-start “hopefully can be good for the industry and make all these companies more productive over time.”  

In May, Musk admitted that not all the employees he fired were superfluous. “Desperate times call for desperate measures,” he [told](https://twitter.com/CNBC/status/1658663628684533761) CNBC. “There’s no question that some of the people who were let go probably shouldn’t have been let go.”

He [told the BBC](https://fortune.com/2023/04/12/elon-musk-twitter-job-cuts-redundancies-layoffs-company-was-going-to-die/) in April that Twitter “was going to go bankrupt if we did not cut costs immediately. This is not a caring-uncaring situation: If the whole ship sinks, then nobody’s got a job.” Musk took on [billions in debt](https://fortune.com/2023/01/18/elon-musk-twitter-sales-revenue-interest-payment-loans-debt/) to finance his takeover, making the situation even more pressing. 

At Meta, Zuckerberg did not face the same kind of financial urgency. 

“It’s a kind of strategy decision and sometimes financially required, but not fully in our case,” he said. “A lot of it was more culturally and strategically driven by this push where I wanted us to become a stronger technology company.”

He explained that he wanted to “empower engineers more, the people who are building things, the technical teams,” and part of that was making sure those employees are “not the leaf nodes of the organization. I don’t want, like, eight levels of management and then the people actually doing the work.”

He added, “I think over time companies just build up very large support functions that are not doing the kind of core technical work, and those functions are very important, but I think having them in the right proportion is important.”

# Mark Zuckerberg backs Elon Musk Silicon Valley decision

Hillary Remy

July 23, 2026 5 min read

A clip from an old Lex Fridman podcast interview with [Mark Zuckerberg](https://www.thestreet.com/tag/mark-zuckerberg) is making the rounds on X (the former Twitter), and the timing of its revival is the most interesting part of the story.

The clip shows Zuckerberg praising [Elon Musk](https://www.thestreet.com/tag/elon-musk)'s overhaul of Twitter at a moment when the two men were in the middle of a very public rivalry. Nobody paid much attention when it aired. People are paying attention now.

The clip [surfaced on X](https://x.com/jaynitx/status/2079244596476006632?s=46) on July 20, and it hit differently than it would have a few years ago. Meta has since gone through versions of the same thing Zuckerberg praised Musk for doing. The question the clip is raising right now is whether it worked.

## **What Zuckerberg said about Musk and the Twitter overhaul**

Speaking on Lex Fridman's podcast, Zuckerberg said Musk's overhaul of Twitter went deeper than simple cost-cutting. Musk had acquired the company for $44 billion and cut the workforce from roughly 8,000 employees to fewer than 2,000 in a matter of months.

Zuckerberg said the more important part was what Musk was trying to build afterward.

**More Mark Zuckerberg:**

*   [**Mark Zuckerberg says infinite money won't make him quit his job**](https://www.thestreet.com/employment/mark-zuckerberg-says-infinite-money-wont-make-him-quit-his-job-employment-meta-ceo)
    
*   [**Mark Zuckerberg makes a move on a new billion-dollar market**](https://www.thestreet.com/latest-news/mark-zuckerberg-makes-a-move-on-a-new-billion-dollar-market-prediction-market-arena)
    
*   [**Mark Zuckerberg admits mistakes in leaked memo after Meta layoffs**](https://www.thestreet.com/employment/mark-zuckerberg-admits-mistakes-in-leaked-memo-after-meta-layoffs)
    

"I do think that Elon led a push early on to make Twitter a lot leaner," he said. "You can agree or disagree with exactly all the tactics, but a lot of the specific principles that he pushed on around basically trying to make the organization more technical, around decreasing the distance between engineers of the company and him, fewer layers of management, I think those were generally good changes."

Musk continues to apply versions of that same philosophy across his companies, [as TheStreet reported](https://www.thestreet.com/technology/elon-musk-and-tesla-announce-serious-ai-changes-for-workers).

Zuckerberg also said Musk gave other tech founders permission to do what they'd wanted to do anyway. "My sense is that there were a lot of other people who thought that those were good changes, but who may have been a little shy about doing them."

He was careful not to offer a full endorsement of everything Musk did. "From the outside, it's very hard to know. Did he cut too much? Did he not cut enough? I don't think it's my place to opine on that."

## **Why Zuckerberg's take on Musk and Twitter is landing differently now**

When Zuckerberg made those comments, Meta was in the middle of its own restructuring. The company cut more than 21,000 jobs in what Zuckerberg called a "year of efficiency," running almost in parallel with the Fridman interview.

# Zuckerberg credits Musk with kicking off tech trend of firing middle managers | Fortune

Mark Zuckerberg is giving credit where credit is due. The Meta CEO believes that Elon Musk, by firing hordes of middle managers at Twitter after his $44 billion takeover last October, kicked off a trend that’s been “good for the industry.” 

After assuming control, Musk laid off thousands of employees, reducing headcount from about 7,500 to less than 2,000 by February of this year, [according to](https://techcrunch.com/2023/05/25/elon-musk-twitter-everything-you-need-to-know/) TechCrunch.

Zuckerberg delivered the comments [on the _Lex Fridman Podcast_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ff4fRgnuFgQ) on Thursday. The way he sees it—and laid-off Twitter employees would surely beg to differ—Musk was right in trying to make the company “more technical” and decrease the distance between engineers and himself, with “fewer layers of management.” 

“His actions led me and I think a lot of other folks in the industry to think about, ‘Hey, are we kind of doing this as much as we should?’” he said. “Could we make our companies better by pushing on some of the same principles?…My sense is that there were a lot of other people who thought that those were good changes, but who may have been a little shy about doing them.” 

It was something Musk “was quite ahead of a bunch of the other companies on,” he added.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, [announced in March](https://fortune.com/2023/03/14/meta-layoffs-10000-mark-zuckerberg-year-of-efficiency-hiring-freeze/) that it would lay off 10,000 employees—adding to the 11,000 job cuts it started last November—and would also freeze hiring on 5,000 more positions. In a [blog post](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/03/mark-zuckerberg-meta-year-of-efficiency/), Zuckerberg said he would “make our organization flatter by removing multiple layers of management,” part of a “year of efficiency.”

While Meta employees have [described “shattered” morale](https://fortune.com/2023/04/20/meta-employees-tech-layoffs-mark-zuckerberg-morale-confidence/), Wall Street has responded positively, with Meta shares up about 112% year to date.

Other big tech companies have [also shed workers this year](https://fortune.com/2023/01/07/salesforce-ceo-marc-benioff-dodges-layoffs-questions-ohana-mantra-questioned/), among them [Salesforce](https://fortune.com/company/salesforce-com/), [Microsoft](https://fortune.com/company/microsoft/), and [Amazon](https://fortune.com/company/amazon-com/). Tech layoffs in 2023 are [the highest they’ve been](https://fortune.com/2023/06/01/tech-layoffs-worst-since-dot-com-bubble-burst/) since the dotcom bubble burst 22 years ago, according to a [report](https://www.challengergray.com/blog/may-2023-layoffs-jump-on-tech-retail-auto-ytd-hiring-lowest-since-2016/) released earlier this month by recruiting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

# Resurfaced viral podcast clip shows Zuckerberg praising Musk’s Twitter layoffs in 2022

A previously overlooked conversation featuring Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg from a three-year-old podcast episode has now gone viral. The clip has been taken from a 2023 episode of Lex Fridman’s podcast and has now been widely shared on X.

Musk had cut more than 6,000 employees after he bought Twitter in 2022, reducing the company’s workforce from 8,000 to just 1,500. According to the clip, Zuckerberg had a positive assessment of the move.

Zuckerberg mentioned that Musk was trying to make Twitter (now X) leaner. “You can agree or disagree with exactly all the tactics, but a lot of the specific principles that he pushed on around basically trying to make the organization more technical, around decreasing the distance between engineers of the company and him, fewer layers of management, I think those were generally good changes,” he said.

Zuckerberg added that he believed the changes were good for the industry because it was others who were likely to have wanted to make the same changes, but they may have been a “little shy about doing them.”

“Just in my conversations with other founders and how people have reacted to the things that we’ve done, what I’ve heard from a lot of folks is when someone like you, when I wrote the letter outlining the organizational changes I wanted to make back in March and when people see what Elon is doing, that gives people the ability to think through how to shape their organizations in a way that can be good for the industry and make all these companies more productive over time,” Zuckerberg [said](https://x.com/jaynitx/status/2079244596476006632).

Zuckerberg noted that he thinks that Musk was “ahead of a bunch of other companies” on this issue. He further added, “Certainly his actions led me and I think a lot of other folks in the industry to think about, hey, are we kind of doing this as much as we should? Could we make our companies better by pushing on some of these same principles?”

He also made it clear that he was not claiming every decision made at Twitter was correct. “From the outside, it’s very hard to know. Did he cut too much? Did he not cut enough? I don’t think it’s my place to opine on that,” Zuckerberg [said](https://www.indiatoday.in/technology/news/story/mark-zuckerberg-elon-musk-twitter-layoffs-resurfaced-podcast-x-2952586-2026-07-21).

These comments may provide insights into Zuckerberg’s own approach to layoffs. In 2023, Zuckerberg described the company’s restructuring as part of Meta’s “year of efficiency,” with the company focusing on reducing costs and simplifying operations. This strategy continued as Meta cut expenses in some areas while increasing investments in artificial intelligence.

Meanwhile, a group of 26 Meta employees has [sued](https://fortune.com/2026/07/15/meta-workers-sue-over-ai-layoff-math/) the company, claiming it used artificial intelligence systems to select people for layoffs, disproportionately targeting those on medical, parental or family leave. They are among the 8,000 employees, or about 10% of its workforce, Meta said it would lay off in May.
